title: Multiorbital Anisotropy and Magnetic Excitations in Trilayer Nickelate Pr$_4$Ni$_3$O$_{10}$
authors: Ziqiang Guan, Sophia F. R. TenHuisen, Xuefei Guo, Wei He, Aulden K. Jones, Marli dos Reis Cantarino, Xinglong Chen, Hong Zheng, J. F. Mitchell, Nicholas B. Brookes, Mark P. M. Dean, Matteo Mitrano
abstract: Rare-earth substitution strongly modifies the structure, metallicity, and superconducting behavior of Ruddlesden-Popper (RP) nickelates, but its impact on their magnetic interactions remains unclear. Here, we combine x-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and resonant inelastic x-ray scattering (RIXS) to resolve the multiorbital electronic structure and magnetic excitations of Pr$_4$Ni$_3$O$_{10}$. The absence of an overlapping rare-earth resonance provides direct access to the Ni $L_3$ edge, while polarization-dependent measurements at the Ni $L$- and O $K$-edges resolve distinct planar and out-of-plane Ni-O hybridization channels. Momentum-resolved RIXS reveals dispersive magnetic excitations that soften toward the incommensurate spin-density-wave wave vector. An effective spin-wave analysis yields a sizable intra-trilayer exchange coupling, comparable to the leading in-plane interactions and robust against rare-earth substitution. Our results identify the multilayer architecture, rather than rare-earth substitution alone, as a key control knob of the magnetic interactions in these materials.
summary: This work uses XAS and RIXS spectroscopy to characterize the electronic structure and magnetic excitations in the trilayer nickelate $	ext{Pr}_4	ext{Ni}_3	ext{O}_{10}$. By analyzing the magnetic response and fitting to spin-wave models, the authors determine that the magnetic interactions are governed by a balanced interplay between in-plane and interlayer couplings, establishing the multilayer architecture as the primary determinant of magnetic behavior.
main_problem: The study aims to understand how the multilayer nickelate architecture controls electronic and magnetic interactions in $	ext{Pr}_4	ext{Ni}_3	ext{O}_{10}$, particularly how rare-earth substitution affects these magnetic couplings.
main_result: The magnetic interactions are governed by a balanced network of significant in-plane and interlayer couplings, suggesting the multilayer structure, rather than rare-earth substitution alone, is the key control knob.
method: The research combines advanced experimental techniques (XAS and polarization-dependent RIXS) with theoretical modeling (Spin-Wave Analysis and fitting to various Hamiltonian models).
model_or_system: The system is the trilayer Ruddlesden-Popper nickelate $	ext{Pr}_4	ext{Ni}_3	ext{O}_{10}$. The analysis models the magnetic interactions using effective exchange couplings ($J_1, J_2, J_3, J_z$) within a spin-wave framework.
key_observables: Dispersive magnetic excitations, orbital hybridization channels (planar vs. out-of-plane), and effective exchange couplings ($J_1, J_2, J_3, J_z$).
important_parameters: Exchange couplings are found to be in the $\sim 10-16 	ext{ meV}$ range, indicating a balanced magnetic network.
main_assumptions: The conventional Linear Spin-Wave Theory (LSWT) is favored as the most direct quantitative description, although comparisons with entangled-dimer and stripe-dimer models were made.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crystal structure and effective magnetic interaction model, while RIXS maps show the momentum and energy dependence of the magnetic response.
paper_structure: The paper first uses XAS/RIXS to map the multiorbital electronic structure and anisotropy. It then uses momentum-resolved RIXS to identify dispersive magnetic excitations softening toward the SDW wave vector. Finally, it employs spin-wave analysis and fitting to various Hamiltonian models to quantify the exchange couplings.
why_interesting: The detailed mapping of magnetic interactions using spectroscopic probes like RIXS provides quantitative insight into the underlying quantum magnetic Hamiltonian, which is crucial for understanding strongly correlated electron behavior in cuprate/nickelate superconductors.
